inept

/in-EPT/ — stress on EPT; rhymes with swept · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Someone who is inept lacks the skill or ability needed to do something well, so their attempts come out clumsy.

An inept juggler, he dropped all three oranges on the first toss.

Worked Example

The inept carpenter hammered the nail through the wall and destroyed the board beneath it.

Inept pinpoints a lack of skill or ability — not just making a single mistake, but demonstrating fundamental incompetence. It's about lacking the skill needed to do something well, which is more precise than just 'bad work.'

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

unskilled: Unskilled is a neutral fact about training: an unskilled worker simply has not been taught the task yet. Inept is a judgment about performance — the attempts themselves come out clumsy and bungled, however much teaching came first. A new hire is unskilled on day one without being inept.

incompetent: Incompetent is the formal verdict that someone cannot perform a job or duty properly — the word an official review would use. Inept is less formal and more vivid: it pictures the bungled attempts themselves, the missed nail and the dropped pass that show the ability just is not there.

clumsy: Clumsy describes awkward physical movement — fumbling fingers, tripping feet, dropped plates — whatever the cause. Inept is about lacking the skill a task needs, so even a graceful dancer can be an inept negotiator. Clumsy names how the body moves; inept names the missing ability.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

adept: highly skilled through practice and natural fit

proficient: capable and competent from solid training

Where it sits · how capable the person is — inept → adequate → skilled → expert

adequate vs. inept: Adequate is a step above inept: an adequate cook gets an edible meal on the table, while an inept cook burns even the toast.

skilled vs. inept: Skilled is far above inept on the ability scale: a skilled juggler keeps every ball in the air, while an inept one drops them all.

expert vs. inept: Expert is the extreme opposite of inept: an expert performs at the highest level, while an inept person can barely manage the basics.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-

Prefix — in-: not, opposite of (Latin)

Root — ept (aptus)

Root — ept (aptus): fitted, suited, proper (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: In- means 'not,' and -ept comes from Latin aptus, 'fitted or suited': someone inept is literally 'not fitted' for the task — lacking the skill or ability to do it well.

Use the root in a new word: aptitude

Use the root in a new word: aptitude: Aptitude — a natural fitness for learning something — comes from the same Latin root aptus, 'fitted,' that inept negates: an inept person shows no aptitude for the task at all.

Word Choice

neutral

Inept is the word for someone who lacks skill or ability — whose attempts come out clumsy or bungling. Use it when someone is fundamentally unsuited to a task, not just when they make a single mistake. It's less formal than 'incompetent' and more precise than 'bad at.'
